toc.title: 5.18 Chemistry in the service of mankind
5.21 Nuclear Chemistry and Applications of Radioactivity

html:
Group A of the Grade 12 Chemistry paper is eleven one-mark questions, all compulsory, and it is the cheapest part of the paper to win if you practise it the right way. This chapter walks through all twenty-one syllabus units in the order of the CDC curriculum. Every unit opens with a one-table digest of the facts the examiner keeps returning to, then sets a block of multiple-choice questions, and closes with an answer key in which each option is justified in one line — including the wrong-answer trap that the distractors were built to catch.

How to read the year tags

A tag such as (NEB 2081) or (NEB 2079 model) means that the question, or the same stem on the same topic, was actually set in that board paper or official model paper. Where the original print was garbled in the source we could reach, the options here are re-set but the stem and the answer are unchanged. Untagged questions are new, written to the syllabus and to the same pattern. There is no published per-unit marks grid for Grade 12 Chemistry, so teaching hours are used as a proxy for weight — not as a promise.

What Group A actually tests

Across the papers of 2078 (model) to 2083, the eleven Group A questions come from six families: an equivalent weight or normality calculation; a Ksp, pH or Ka calculation; the order of a reaction from its half-life or rate law; a comparison of E° values; an identification of a transition-metal or heavy-metal fact; and the product of a named organic reaction. Organic chemistry carries 55 of the 128 teaching hours, and about seven of the eleven questions. Do each numerical on paper before you look at the options: the wrong options are built from arithmetic slips, not from ignorance of the chemistry.

5.1 Volumetric Analysis

Idea What you must be able to state
Equivalent weight molar mass ÷ n-factor; the n-factor is the H⁺ or OH⁻ replaced, or the electrons exchanged, in that reaction
Acid M ÷ basicity actually used (H₃PO₃ is dibasic; H₃PO₂ is monobasic)
Base M ÷ acidity actually used
Salt M ÷ total positive (or negative) charge
Oxidant or reductant M ÷ electrons gained or lost per formula unit
KMnO₄ 158/5 = 31.6 in acid; 158/3 = 52.7 in neutral or weak alkali; 158/1 = 158 in strong alkali
K₂Cr₂O₇ in acid 294/6 = 49
Oxalic acid crystals, H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O M = 126, so equivalent weight = 63
Molarity moles of solute per litre of solution; changes with temperature
Molality moles of solute per kg of solvent; independent of temperature

ppm mg of solute per kg of solution, which is mg L⁻¹ for dilute aqueous solutions
Primary standard pure, stable, non-hygroscopic, high molar mass, exact formula: oxalic acid crystals, anhydrous Na₂CO₃, K₂Cr₂O₇
Secondary standard standardised against a primary one: NaOH, HCl, KMnO₄, Na₂S₂O₃
Normality equation N₁V₁ = N₂V₂ at the end point
Indicators strong acid–strong base: phenolphthalein or methyl orange; strong acid–weak base (Na₂CO₃): methyl orange; weak acid–strong base: phenolphthalein; KMnO₄ is its own indicator
Mohr's method Cl⁻ estimated with standard AgNO₃ and K₂CrO₄ indicator (brick-red Ag₂CrO₄ at the end point)

  4. For the titration of H₂SO₄ against Na₂CO₃ the indicator to be recommended is (NEB model set A) [1]amethyl orangebphenolphthaleinclitmus paperdstarch
  5. The equivalent weight of K₂Cr₂O₇ (M = 294) acting as an oxidising agent in acidic medium is [1]a294b98c49d42
  6. The equivalent weight of KMnO₄ (M = 158) in acidic medium is [1]a158b79c52.7d31.6
  7. A liquor ammonia sample is 25 % (w/w) NH₃ and has specific gravity 0.91. Its molarity is (NEB 2079 model) [1]a13.4 Mb14.7 Mc25 Md6.7 M
  8. 100 cc of N/2 HCl, 20 cc of N/10 HNO₃ and 50 cc of N/5 H₂SO₄ are mixed. The pH of the mixture is about (NEB model set A) [1]a0.30b0.44c0.56d1.00
  9. 3.15 g of oxalic acid crystals (H₂C₂O₄·2H₂O) are dissolved to make 500 mL of solution. Its normality is (NEB 2083) [1]a0.05 Nb0.10 Nc0.20 Nd0.50 N
  10. Which of the following is a primary standard substance? [1]aNaOHbKMnO₄cHCldoxalic acid crystals
  11. In the titration of oxalic acid against KMnO₄ in acidic medium the indicator is [1]aphenolphthaleinbmethyl orangecKMnO₄ itselfdstarch

Answers — Volumetric Analysis

1. (b) — H₃PO₃ is dibasic, and here both replaceable H are used (Na₂HPO₃), so E = 82/2 = 41. Option (a) forgets to divide; (c) divides by 3 because the formula has three H, but one of them is bonded to P and is not acidic.

2. (a) — 5 g per 100 mL = 50 g L⁻¹; equivalent weight = 106/2 = 53; N = 50/53 = 0.94. Option (c) is the molarity (50/106), which forgets the n-factor, and (d) doubles the n-factor.

3. (d) — Cl⁻ + Ag⁺ → AgCl↓. This is precipitation titration (Mohr's method), with K₂CrO₄ only as the indicator, so K₂CrO₄ alone cannot be the titrant.

4. (a) — Na₂CO₃ is a weak base; at complete neutralisation the solution holds H₂CO₃ (pH about 4), which methyl orange signals. Phenolphthalein changes colour at the half-way stage, NaHCO₃, so it would give a wrong end point.

5. (c) — Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O takes six electrons, so E = 294/6 = 49. Option (b) uses three electrons, the n-factor of dilute-acid reduction of a different oxidant.

6. (d) — MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O, so E = 158/5 = 31.6. Option (c) is the neutral-medium value (three electrons).

7. (a) — M = (10 × 0.91 × 25)/17 = 227.5/17 = 13.4 mol L⁻¹. Option (d) uses 34 as the molar mass, which is 2 × 17.

8. (b) — equivalents = 100 × 0.5 + 20 × 0.1 + 50 × 0.2 = 50 + 2 + 10 = 62 milli-equivalents in 170 mL, so N = 0.3647 and pH = −log 0.3647 = 0.44. Option (c) is the pH if the volumes were forgotten and the three normalities were simply averaged.

9. (b) — E = 126/2 = 63; N = (3.15/63)/0.5 = 0.05/0.5 = 0.10 N. Option (a) forgets that the volume is 0.5 L, not 1 L.

10. (d) — oxalic acid crystals are pure, stable and of exactly known formula. NaOH absorbs CO₂ and water, HCl is volatile, and KMnO₄ is reduced by traces of organic matter, so all three are secondary standards.

11. (c) — one drop of excess MnO₄⁻ makes the solution permanently pink, so KMnO₄ is a self-indicator. The solution is warmed to about 60–70 °C because the first reaction is slow at room temperature, and dilute H₂SO₄ supplies the H⁺ the half-reaction needs.

12. (b) — N₁V₁ = N₂V₂ gives N₂ = (0.100 × 25.0)/20.0 = 0.125 N. Option (a) inverts the ratio of the volumes.

5.2 Ionic Equilibrium

Idea What you must be able to state
Brønsted–Lowry acid / base proton donor / proton acceptor; every acid has a conjugate base, and the stronger the acid the weaker its conjugate base
Lewis acid / base electron-pair acceptor (BF₃, AlCl₃, H⁺) / donor (NH₃, OH⁻, H₂O)
Ostwald's dilution law Ka = Cα²/(1 − α) ≈ Cα², so α = √(Ka/C); α rises on dilution; it fails for strong electrolytes
Ionic product of water Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C; it increases with temperature, because ionisation is endothermic
pH and pOH pH = −log[H⁺]; pH + pOH = 14 at 25 °C
pH of a weak acid [H⁺] = √(KaC) = Cα
Solubility product AB: Ksp = s²; AB₂ or A₂B: Ksp = 4s³, so s = (Ksp/4)^(1/3)

Common ion effect adding a common ion lowers the solubility of a sparingly soluble salt and suppresses the ionisation of a weak electrolyte

Salt hydrolysis strong acid + strong base: neutral; weak acid + strong base: alkaline; strong acid + weak base: acidic

  1. The pH of 10⁻⁸ M aqueous HCl at 25 °C is (NEB 2079) [1]a8b7cslightly less than 7dmore than 8
  2. Equal volumes of 1 M NaNO₃ and 1 M KCl are mixed. The concentration of nitrate ions in the mixture is (NEB 2079) [1]a0.25 Mb0.5 Mc1 Md2 M
  3. The ionic product of water at 393 K is (NEB 2083) [1]agreater than 1 × 10⁻¹⁴bless than 1 × 10⁻¹⁴cequal to 1 × 10⁻¹⁴dequal to 1 × 10⁻⁷
  4. The pH of 10 mL of 1 × 10⁻⁷ M H₂SO₄ at 25 °C is (NEB model set B) [1]aexactly 7.00b6.62c7.30d6.70
  5. The solubility product of chalk (CaCO₃, M = 100) is 9.3 × 10⁻⁸. Its solubility is about (NEB 2078 model) [1]a3.05 × 10⁻⁴ g L⁻¹b3.05 × 10⁻² g L⁻¹c9.3 × 10⁻⁸ g L⁻¹d0.93 g L⁻¹
  6. For a sparingly soluble salt A₂B the solubility s is related to Ksp by (NEB model set A) [1]as = Ksp^(1/2)bs = (Ksp/2)^(1/3)cs = (Ksp/4)^(1/3)ds = (Ksp/27)^(1/4)
  7. The degree of ionisation of 0.01 M HCN (Ka = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁰) is (NEB 2082) [1]a2.2 × 10⁻⁴b4.8 × 10⁻⁸c2.2 × 10⁻²d6.9 × 10⁻⁶
  8. A 0.1 M solution of ethanoic acid is 1.34 % ionised. Its dissociation constant is (NEB 2079 model) [1]a1.8 × 10⁻⁵b1.34 × 10⁻³c1.8 × 10⁻³d1.34 × 10⁻⁵
  9. A solution of KOH has pH 8. It is diluted 1000 times. The pH of the diluted solution is (NEB 2078 model) [1]a5b11c8djust above 7
  10. A buffer contains 0.2 M ethanoic acid and 0.1 M sodium ethanoate (pKa = 4.74). Its pH is [1]a4.74b5.04c4.44d4.14
  11. The conjugate base of H₂PO₄⁻ is [1]aH₃PO₄bHPO₄²⁻cPO₄³⁻dOH⁻
  12. Equal volumes of 2 × 10⁻⁴ M BaCl₂ and 2 × 10⁻⁴ M Na₂SO₄ are mixed (Ksp of BaSO₄ = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰). A precipitate [1]aforms, because the ionic product is 1 × 10⁻⁸bdoes not form, because the ionic product is 4 × 10⁻⁸cdoes not form, because both salts are solubledforms only on heating
  13. The aqueous solution of sodium ethanoate is [1]aacidicbalkalinecneutraldamphoteric
Answers — Ionic Equilibrium

1. (c) — the acid contributes 10⁻⁸ M H⁺, but water supplies about 9.5 × 10⁻⁸ M more, so [H⁺] = 1.05 × 10⁻⁷ and pH = 6.98. An acid can never give a pH of 8, which is the trap in option (a).

2. (b) — mixing doubles the volume and NaNO₃ is diluted from 1 M to 0.5 M. Neither KCl nor the spectator ions contribute nitrate. Option (c) forgets the dilution.

3. (a) — ionisation of water is endothermic, so Kw rises with temperature (about 3.8 × 10⁻¹³ at 100 °C). Kw = 10⁻¹⁴ is valid only at 25 °C.

4. (b) — [H⁺] from the acid is 2 × 10⁻⁷ and water adds a little more: [H⁺]² − 2 × 10⁻⁷[H⁺] − 10⁻¹⁴ = 0, so [H⁺] = 2.41 × 10⁻⁷ and pH = 6.62. Option (a) ignores the fact that H₂SO₄ gives two H⁺.

5. (b) — s = √(9.3 × 10⁻⁸) = 3.05 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹; multiplying by M = 100 gives 3.05 × 10⁻² g L⁻¹. Option (a) stops at mol L⁻¹.

6. (c) — A₂B gives 2s of A⁺ and s of B²⁻, so Ksp = (2s)²(s) = 4s³.

7. (a) — α = √(Ka/C) = √(4.8 × 10⁻¹⁰/0.01) = √(4.8 × 10⁻⁸) = 2.2 × 10⁻⁴. Option (c) uses √Ka alone.

8. (a) — Ka ≈ Cα² = 0.1 × (0.0134)² = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵. Option (d) squares only part of the expression.

9. (d) — 10⁻⁶ M OH⁻ becomes 10⁻⁹ M, which is far below the 10⁻⁷ M that water itself supplies, so the solution is essentially neutral: [OH⁻] = 1.005 × 10⁻⁷, pH = 7.002. A base can never be diluted into an acid (option a).

10. (c) — pH = 4.74 + log(0.1/0.2) = 4.74 − 0.30 = 4.44. Option (b) inverts the ratio of salt to acid.

11. (b) — the conjugate base is formed by removing one proton: H₂PO₄⁻ → HPO₄²⁻ + H⁺. Option (a) is the conjugate acid.

12. (a) — after mixing, [Ba²⁺] = [SO₄²⁻] = 1 × 10⁻⁴ M, so Qsp = 10⁻⁸ > 10⁻¹⁰ and BaSO₄ precipitates. Option (b) forgets to halve each concentration.

13. (b) — CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻; the salt of a weak acid and a strong base hydrolyses to an alkaline solution.

5.3 Chemical Kinetics

Idea What you must be able to state
Rate law determined experimentally; it is never read off the balanced equation
Order sum of the powers of concentration in the experimental rate law; can be 0, fractional or negative
Molecularity number of species colliding in one elementary step; always 1, 2 or 3 — never zero or fractional
2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂ rate = k[N₂O₅]: first order, although the coefficient is 2
2HI → H₂ + I₂ (on gold) zero order, although two molecules react
Unit of k, zero order mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
Unit of k, first order s⁻¹ (independent of concentration unit)
Unit of k, second order L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹
First-order integrated form k = (2.303/t) log(a/(a−x))
First-order half-life t½ = 0.693/k — independent of initial concentration
Zero-order half-life t½ = a/2k — proportional to initial concentration
Arrhenius equation k = Ae^(−Ea/RT); ln k against 1/T is a straight line of slope −Ea/R
Temperature coefficient rate roughly doubles for each 10 °C rise
Catalyst lowers Ea by offering a new path; does not change ΔH, ΔG or K
Activated complex the highest-energy arrangement at the top of the barrier
Homogeneous / heterogeneous / enzyme NO + O₂ with NO₂; Haber process on Fe; sucrase on sucrose

  1. The rate of a reaction doubles for every 10 °C rise in temperature. The rate at 100 °C compared with that at 10 °C is greater by a factor of (NEB 2079 model) [1]a128b256c512d1024
  2. For a first-order reaction the rate is 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ when the rate constant is 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹. The concentration of the reactant is (NEB 2078 model) [1]a0.8 mol L⁻¹b1.25 mol L⁻¹c0.4 mol L⁻¹d8.0 mol L⁻¹
  3. For a certain reaction the rate is equal to the rate constant. The order of the reaction is (NEB 2081) [1]azerobonectwodthree
  4. The half-life of a reaction is 50 s and does not depend on the initial concentration. The reaction is of (NEB 2082) [1]azero orderbfirst ordercsecond orderdthird order
  5. For 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂ the experimental rate law is rate = k[N₂O₅]. The order is [1]a0b1c2d3
  6. Which of the following can never be zero or fractional? [1]aorderbmolecularitycratedrate constant
  7. The unit of the rate constant of a second-order reaction is [1]as⁻¹bmol L⁻¹ s⁻¹cL mol⁻¹ s⁻¹dL² mol⁻² s⁻¹
  8. In the energy-profile diagram above, a catalyst changes [1]aΔH onlybEa onlycboth Ea and ΔHdneither
  9. In the Arrhenius plot of ln k against 1/T, the slope is [1]a−Ea/RbEa/Rc−Ea/2.303Rdln A
  10. A first-order reaction is 50 % complete in 10 s. The time for it to be 90 % complete is about [1]a18 sb20 sc33 sd50 s
  11. The action of sucrase on sucrose is an example of [1]ahomogeneous catalysisbheterogeneous catalysiscenzyme catalysisdautocatalysis
Answers — Chemical Kinetics

1. (c) — the rise is 90 °C, that is nine steps of 10 °C, so the factor is 2⁹ = 512. Option (d) comes from counting ten steps instead of nine.

2. (a) — rate = k[A], so [A] = 2.4 × 10⁻⁵ / 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ = 0.8 mol L⁻¹.

3. (a) — rate = k[A]⁰ = k only when the exponent is zero; the rate is then independent of concentration.

4. (b) — only for first order is t½ = 0.693/k, with no concentration term. For zero order t½ ∝ a and for second order t½ ∝ 1/a.

5. (b) — order comes from the experimental rate law, not from the balancing coefficients. Option (c) is the classic error of reading the 2 in 2N₂O₅ as the order.

6. (b) — molecularity counts the molecules colliding in a single elementary step, so it must be a whole number 1, 2 or 3. Order is an experimental quantity and may be zero or fractional.

7. (c) — the general unit is mol^(1−n) L^(n−1) s⁻¹; putting n = 2 gives L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹.

8. (b) — a catalyst opens a lower-energy route, lowering Ea in both directions, but reactants and products are unchanged so ΔH, ΔG and K are untouched.

9. (a) — ln k = ln A − Ea/RT. Option (c) would be the slope of a log₁₀ k plot.

10. (c) — k = 0.693/10 = 0.0693 s⁻¹, and t = (2.303/k) log 10 = 2.303/0.0693 = 33.2 s. It is not simply 5 × t½.

11. (c) — sucrase is an enzyme, a biological catalyst; the substrate must fit its active site.

5.4 Thermodynamics

Statement Form / value
First law ΔU = q + w (w is work done on the system)
Isochoric process ΔV = 0, so w = 0 and q(v) = ΔU
Isobaric process q(p) = ΔH
Adiabatic process q = 0, so ΔU = w
Isothermal process ΔT = 0, so ΔU = 0 and q = −w
Cyclic process ΔU = 0 and ΔH = 0 (both are state functions)
Free expansion into vacuum p(ext) = 0, so w = 0
Relation of ΔH and ΔU ΔH = ΔU + Δn(g)RT
Exothermic reaction ΔH negative; heat leaves the system
Endothermic reaction ΔH positive; heat enters the system
Hess's law ΔH of a reaction is the same by any route
Enthalpy of neutralisation, strong acid + strong base −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹ (always, because it is really H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O)
Second law entropy of the universe increases in every spontaneous change
Entropy order S(gas) > S(liquid) > S(solid)
Gibbs equation ΔG = ΔH − TΔS
Spontaneity criterion ΔG < 0 spontaneous; ΔG = 0 equilibrium; ΔG > 0 non-spontaneous
ΔH −, ΔS + spontaneous at all temperatures
ΔH +, ΔS − non-spontaneous at all temperatures
ΔG° and K ΔG° = −2.303RT log K; K > 1 needs ΔG° negative

  2. According to the Gibbs–Helmholtz equation, a process is spontaneous when (NEB 2082) [1]aΔG is positivebΔG is negativecΔG is zerodΔH is negative
  3. For a reaction at equilibrium, [1]aΔG = 0bΔG° = 0cΔH = 0dΔS = 0
  4. For an endothermic reaction [1]aΔH is negativebΔH is positivecΔU is zerodq is negative
  5. The heat absorbed by a system at constant volume is equal to [1]aΔHbΔUcΔGdΔS
  6. In an adiabatic process [1]aq = 0bw = 0cΔT = 0dΔU = 0
  7. For a cyclic process the change in internal energy is [1]aalways positivebalways negativeczerodequal to q
  8. The law that allows an unmeasurable enthalpy change to be obtained by adding known ones is [1]aHess's lawbLaplace's lawcfirst lawdRaoult's law
  9. Which has the highest entropy per mole? [1]aicebwatercsteamddry ice
  10. A reaction with ΔH negative and ΔS positive is [1]aspontaneous at all temperaturesbspontaneous only at low Tcspontaneous only at high Tdnever spontaneous
  11. If the equilibrium constant of a reaction is greater than 1, then ΔG° is [1]apositivebnegativeczerodequal to ΔH°
  12. The enthalpy of neutralisation of HCl by NaOH is −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹. For HNO₃ and KOH it is [1]a−57.1 kJ mol⁻¹b−114.2 kJ mol⁻¹c−28.5 kJ mol⁻¹dless negative
  13. The work done when a gas expands into a vacuum is [1]amaximumbzerocinfinitedequal to −ΔU
Answers — Thermodynamics

1. (b) — reverse the second equation and add it to the first: C + O₂ → CO₂ (−x) plus CO₂ → CO + ½O₂ (+y) gives C + ½O₂ → CO, so ΔHf = (y − x) kJ. Option (a) is the trap of adding the two combustion enthalpies instead of subtracting.

2. (b) — spontaneity is decided by the sign of ΔG at the actual conditions. Option (d) is the common trap: an exothermic reaction can still be non-spontaneous if TΔS opposes it strongly enough.

3. (a) — at equilibrium ΔG = 0. ΔG° is a fixed number for the standard state and equals −2.303RT log K, which is zero only in the special case K = 1.

4. (b) — the system absorbs heat, so its enthalpy rises and ΔH > 0. Sign conventions are worth one mark almost every year.

5. (b) — at constant volume no expansion work is done, so all the heat goes into internal energy.

6. (a) — "adiabatic" means no heat crosses the boundary; work may still be done, so ΔU is not zero.

7. (c) — internal energy is a state function and the system returns to its initial state.

8. (a) — Hess's law of constant heat summation, a direct consequence of enthalpy being a state function.

9. (c) — gases have far more positional and thermal disorder than liquids or solids. Dry ice is solid CO₂.

10. (a) — ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative for every T when ΔH < 0 and ΔS > 0.

11. (b) — from ΔG° = −2.303RT log K, log K > 0 requires ΔG° < 0.

12. (a) — both are strong acid plus strong base, so the reaction is the same one, H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

13. (b) — work = −p(ext)ΔV and the external pressure is zero, so no work is done however large the expansion.

Inorganic Chemistry — the costliest confusion

"All transition metals and their compounds are coloured" is false, and zinc is not a transition element at all. Colour needs partially filled d orbitals for a d–d transition, so Sc³⁺ (3d⁰), Ti⁴⁺ (3d⁰), Cu⁺ (3d¹⁰) and Zn²⁺ (3d¹⁰) are all colourless. Zn, Cd and Hg have a complete d¹⁰ shell in the atom and in every stable ion they form, so by the IUPAC definition they are not transition elements — they sit in the d block but are not of it.

Applied Chemistry — the costliest confusion

Gypsum does not make cement set faster; it slows it down. About 2–3 % of calcium sulphate is ground in with the clinker purely to retard the flash set caused by tricalcium aluminate, so that the concrete can be transported and placed. The same trap appears in the paper unit: pulping removes lignin, not cellulose, and it is the removal of lignin that lets the cellulose fibres bond to one another.

Chapter summary

  • Group A is 11 questions for 11 marks, all compulsory, and in the most recent sittings the booklet is distributed thirty minutes into the paper, with the answers written on the ordinary answer sheet.
  • Six families cover most of Group A in Chemistry: equivalent weight, Ksp and pH, order of reaction, comparison of E° values, reagent identification, and the products of named organic reactions.
  • Equivalent weight = molar mass ÷ valency factor. The valency factor is the electrons transferred, or the replaceable H⁺ or OH⁻, in that particular reaction — not the valency of the metal.
  • Order is experimental, molecularity is mechanistic. Never read the order off the balanced equation, and never let molecularity be zero or fractional.
  • In a galvanic cell the anode is negative; in electrolysis it is positive. Oxidation happens at the anode in both.
  • Colour in transition-metal compounds needs a partly filled d subshell, so Sc³⁺ and Zn²⁺ are colourless — and zinc is not a transition element at all.
  • In organic chemistry the reagent and the medium decide the product: aqueous versus alcoholic KOH, KCN versus AgCN, and the six different media for reducing nitrobenzene.
  • Phenol dissolves in NaOH but not in NaHCO₃; a carboxylic acid dissolves in both, with effervescence. That single line separates them.
  • A positive iodoform test needs a CH₃CO– or CH₃CH(OH)– group; Tollens' and Fehling's separate aldehydes from ketones, and benzaldehyde is the standing exception to Fehling's.
  • Work every numerical MCQ on paper to one decimal place before you look at the options — the distractors are built from the arithmetic slips, not from ignorance of the chemistry.
